# gh-upload

File hosting backed by a git repository. Upload a file, get a permanent public
URL back. Intended for delivering build artifacts, reports, logs and other
files to people or agents that need a link.

## Fast path

Preferred: fetch and run the uploader this server hosts. It splits large files
correctly and reads the server's limits, so it cannot drift out of sync.

    export GH_UPLOAD_URL="<the server URL you were given>"
    export GH_UPLOAD_TOKEN="<the access token you were given>"

    curl -fsSL "$GH_UPLOAD_URL/upload.sh" -o upload.sh
    bash upload.sh /path/to/file
    # -> prints the download URL on stdout; progress goes to stderr

Small files also work with plain curl:

    curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $GH_UPLOAD_TOKEN" \
         -F "file=@/path/to/file" "$GH_UPLOAD_URL/api/v1/files"

## Read this before doing it yourself

**Do not POST a large file to `/api/v1/files` in one request.** A body larger
than `max_simple_upload` is rejected with HTTP 413 by the CDN in front of the
server, and that response comes from the CDN as **HTML, not JSON** — so a JSON
parser will fail on it rather than give you a useful error. Files above that
size must be split and sent through `/api/v1/files/chunks` + `/complete`, which
is what `upload.sh` does.

**Ask the server for its limits rather than assuming them:**

    curl -sS "$GH_UPLOAD_URL/api/v1/config"

    {
      "code": 0,
      "data": {
        "api_base_url": "https://...",          # public base; use this for links
        "upload_url": "https://.../api/v1/files",
        "chunk_size": 16777216,                 # bytes per chunk
        "max_simple_upload": 16777216           # largest single-request upload
      }
    }

**Concurrency is limited server-side.** Sending many chunks at once is fine and
is what the script does, but the server admits only a few at a time and answers
HTTP 503 with `"retryable": true` for the rest. Honour that: back off briefly
and resend the same chunk. A retry is always safe — see Idempotency.

## Authentication

Writes require the access token: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

Reads do **not**. The download URL is the deliverable, so it stays openable by
whoever receives the link. Do not append the token to a shared URL.

If the server has no token configured, every write returns HTTP 503 saying so,
and writes are impossible until an operator sets one. This is intentional: an
unconfigured token must not silently mean "no protection".

## Errors

Every failure is JSON with an HTTP status code, never a 200 carrying a failure:

    { "code": -1, "msg": "human readable reason", "retryable": true|false }

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 400 | The request is malformed | Fix the request; retrying will not help |
| 401 | Missing or wrong access token | Check `GH_UPLOAD_TOKEN` |
| 404 | No such file id | Check the id |
| 413 | Body too large | Split the file and use the chunk endpoints |
| 502 | The git backend failed upstream | Retry — usually transient |
| 503 | Server shedding load, or writes disabled | If `msg` mentions overload, back off and retry; if it mentions `ADMIN_TOKEN`, stop and tell the operator |

Branch on the HTTP status, not on `code`. `retryable` is an explicit signal for
the cases where a retry is worthwhile.

## Idempotency and retries

Retrying is safe and will not produce duplicates:

- Chunks are written as content-addressed git blobs, so re-sending identical
  bytes resolves to the same object.
- The file's identity is derived from its chunk ids, not from a client-supplied
  value, so the same file always lands on the same id.
- The final commit is a single atomic ref update. A partial upload is never
  visible: either the whole file exists or none of it does.

An interrupted `upload.sh` can simply be re-run.

## Uploading the same content twice

Identity is derived from content, not from the filename or the upload session.
Two uploads with identical bytes produce the **same `file_id`**, so the second
replaces the first's manifest and `GET /api/v1/files` shows one entry — with the
name from the most recent upload. This is intended (it is what makes retries
safe), but it means you cannot store two files with identical content under
different names.

To keep several versions, vary the content or the name in a way that changes the
bytes. A file's size and bytes are what identify it, not its name.

## API reference

All responses are `{"code": 0, "data": ...}` on success and the error shape
above on failure. `{auth}` marks the endpoints needing the bearer token.

    GET  /api/v1/config
    GET  /api/version
    GET  /health

    POST /api/v1/files                        {auth}
      multipart/form-data, field "file"
      -> {name, size, content_hash, content_type, download_url}
      Fails with 413 above max_simple_upload.

    POST /api/v1/files/chunks                 {auth}
      ?upload_id=<32 hex chars>&index=<1..total>&total=<n>
      Body: raw bytes (Content-Type: application/octet-stream)
      -> {upload_id, index, size, sha256, blob_sha}
      Every chunk except the last must be exactly chunk_size bytes.
      upload_id is any 32-character hex string you choose; it only labels the
      session. Retries may reuse it.
      HTTP 503 here means overload: back off and resend.

    POST /api/v1/files/complete               {auth}
      {"original_name": "report.pdf",
       "size": 41943040,
       "total_chunks": 3,
       "content_type": "application/pdf",     (optional)
       "chunks": ["<blob_sha>", "<blob_sha>", "<blob_sha>"]}
      -> {file_id, name, size, content_hash, download_url}
      Send the blob ids in order; chunk entries may be bare strings or the
      objects returned by /chunks. Do not send sizes — the server derives them
      from `size`, and a wrong value would corrupt the file rather than error.

    GET  /api/v1/files
      -> {list: [{name, size, timestamp, download_url, content_hash?}]}
      Newest first. `timestamp` is unix seconds.

    GET  /api/v1/files/<file_id>
      -> metadata for a chunked upload: {file_id, name, size, content_hash,
         hash_algorithm, content_type, created_at, total_chunks, download_url}

    GET  /api/v1/files/<file_id>/download
      -> the file bytes, no auth required

    POST /api/v1/clear                        {auth}
      DESTRUCTIVE: deletes the ENTIRE repository and every file in it. There is
      no per-file delete. Never call this unless explicitly instructed to remove
      everything.

## content_hash

`content_hash` identifies a file. It is the sha256 of the ordered chunk blob
ids, which is **not** the sha256 of the file bytes — clients never hash the file
(a browser cannot hash a stream, so it would have to buffer all of it). The
manifest records this as `hash_algorithm: "sha256-git-blob-ids-v1"`.

Use it to compare two uploads for sameness. Do not present it as a checksum of
the file's contents.

## Verifying a download

The server checks chunk integrity when streaming, and each download sets an
exact `Content-Length`, so a truncated transfer is detectable:

    curl -fsSL -o out.bin "$DOWNLOAD_URL"
    # compare byte count against the "size" reported at upload time

## Notes for agents

- The download URL is public and permanent. Treat it as the deliverable.
- Do not re-upload unchanged files: the id is content-derived, and the same
  content lands on the same id.
- There is no TTL and no per-file delete. Uploaded files accumulate; ask an
  operator to clear the repository if that matters.
